name: Convention of States Caucus (state legislators)
description: Caucus of pro-convention state legislators formed July 2015 (per CRS); was expected to propose draft convention rules at the ALEC San Diego meeting.

name: State Legislators' Article V Caucus
parent_or_affiliation: Later run as a newsletter program under the National Federalism Commission
description: Network of state legislators promoting state-initiated amendments; twice-monthly newsletter (Edition 11 dated Dec 26 2013) produced by Colorado Sen. Kevin Lundberg and New Mexico Rep. Yvette Herrell; official site ArticleVCaucus.com; P.O. Box in Berthoud CO. The newsletter is now published by the NFC as 'Providing Article V / Federalism News and Scholarly Resources Since 2013' and argues the 34-state threshold was met in 1979. || Network of state legislators that publishes a newsletter (edition 11 by Dec 26 2013) and encourages states to adopt Article V convention resolutions. CRS (2017) drew on the newsletter for its application tracking. Its advocacy-organizations page lists Balanced Budget Now!, Bill of Financial Responsibilities Project, Campaign Constitution, Countermand Amendment, Convention of States, Let Us Vote for a Fiscal Responsibility Amendment, Path to Reform, Phoenix Correspondence Commission, U.S. Term Limits and Wolf-Pac. CRS (2017) separately notes a 'Convention of States Caucus' founded by COS in July 2015, a different body.
key_people: Sen. Kevin Lundberg (CO); Rep. Yvette Herrell (NM); W. Bruce Lee (NFC executive director, current)

name: Assembly of State Legislatures (ASL)
parent_or_affiliation: Successor to the Mount Vernon Assembly
role_title: Interstate legislator assembly drafting convention rules
description: Bipartisan body of state legislators (many officially appointed by legislative leaders) drafting rules for a future Article V convention. Committees chose one state/one vote and Mason's Manual. Met at Mount Vernon (Dec 2013), Indianapolis (June 12-13 2014, 33 states, 100+ legislators) and Salt Lake City (Nov 11-13 2015, 80+ legislators from ~30 states) where it failed to adopt final rules over vote allocation; next site (Albany or Philadelphia) undecided. Later activity not verified. || Bipartisan body of sitting state legislators, many formally appointed by their chambers, that grew out of the Dec 7 2013 Mount Vernon Assembly. It met in Indianapolis (June 2014), Washington DC (Dec 2014) and Salt Lake City (Nov 2015), and issued suggested Article V convention rules in June 2016; its committees had chosen one state/one vote and Mason's Manual as the base at the June 2014 meeting. Natelson (i2i) later called it 'apparently defunct'.
key_people: Rep./Sen. Chris Kapenga (WI; co-president); Sen. David Long (IN); Rep. Matt Huffman (OH; presiding officer of general sessions 2014); Rep. Gary Banz (OK); Senate President Wayne Niederhauser (UT; executive committee); Sen. Robert Karnes (WV)

name: Bill of Federalism / Repeal Amendment campaign
description: Randy Barnett's Repeal Amendment would let two-thirds of the states repeal any federal law or regulation (Wikipedia, secondary). His Bill of Federalism (draft published May 13 2009) comes with a model resolution asking Congress to call an Article V convention to propose its amendments. The Bill of Federalism Project was a Tennessee non-profit corporation.

name: Citizens Flag Alliance
description: Founded 1989 by the American Legion (as the Citizens' Flag Honor Guard); incorporated June 1994; over 140 member organizations backing a flag-protection amendment.

name: Coalition Statement Opposing an Article V Convention (Common Cause, 2017; signers updated 2019)
description: Standing coalition statement signed by 200+ national and state organizations (NAACP, AFL-CIO, LWVUS, Sierra Club, Brennan Center, CAP, Democracy 21, SEIU, PFAW among them) opposing any Article V convention. Released April 2017; the signer list was updated March 2019.

name: Common Cause Article V rescission campaign (2016-present)
description: Common Cause's state-by-state effort to block new applications and pass blanket rescissions. Claims credit for removing 12 states in a decade (DE, MD, NV, NM, CO, NJ, IL, OR, NY, then WA, CT, CA in 2025). Common Cause RI says the org has opposed a convention 'since the 1980s'.
key_people: Karen Hobert Flynn; Virginia Kase Solomon

name: Constitutional Rights and Public Interest Groups coalition letter (April 14, 2017)
description: Letter signed by 230 national, state and local organizations urging legislatures to reject convention calls and rescind existing applications; framed around the BBA drive being 'dangerously close' to 34 and the absence of rules limiting a convention.
key_people: Karen Hobert Flynn (Common Cause); Fred Wertheimer (Democracy 21); Robert Greenstein (CBPP)
funding_notes: Release says the BBA convention push is 'bankrolled by billionaires like the Koch Brothers' and led by ALEC

name: ERAmerica
description: Coalition of organizations that led ERA ratification efforts with NOW.

name: John Birch Society rescission campaign (late 1980s-present)
description: JBS says its 'members and allies' have led rescission efforts 'since the late 1980s'; urges rescission in 26 states it counts as having live BBA applications. Maine JBS members lobbied Augusta for rescission in 2011.

name: Let Us Vote for a Balanced Budget Amendment (LUVBBA)
description: Campaign for a BBA convention with three demands: Congress must count existing BBA applications, require ratification by elected state conventions, and refuse to forward any amendment outside the BBA scope. An ALEC model resolution of the same name was finalized Dec 26 2018.

name: Let Us Vote for a Fiscal Responsibility Amendment Campaign
parent_or_affiliation: State Legislators Article V Caucus (listed partner)
description: Lobbies Congress to choose ratification by state conventions with elected, pledged delegates for a future fiscal responsibility amendment. Website returned 503 when checked. Its website (Sept 2024 Wayback copy) is copyrighted by Let Us Vote for a Balanced Budget Amendment Citizen's Campaign, Inc., the LUVBBA entity.

name: Move to Amend
description: Founded 2010 after Citizens United by organizers from WILPF and POCLAD; pushes the 'We the People' Amendment (H.J.Res. 54 in the 116th Congress) through Congress, local resolutions and ballot measures. Wikipedia: 840+ local governments and 22 states passed supporting resolutions (Nov 2023). || Grassroots coalition for the 'We the People Amendment' (H.J.Res. 54 in the 116th Congress) through Congress. Claims (Nov 2023) 840+ local government resolutions, 22 states with passed resolutions or ordinances, and 300+ voter-approved ballot initiatives.
key_people: David Cobb; Ben Manski; Riki Ott; Greg Coleridge; Jennie Spanos

name: The Article V Coalition
description: Coalition of advocates supporting various Article V initiatives, listed by Path To Reform with a YouTube channel; no further detail verified.

name: 16th Biennial General Assembly of the States (1962)
description: CSG assembly that in Dec 1962 endorsed the three amendments, including removal of reapportionment from federal judicial jurisdiction. Held in Chicago Dec 6-7, 1962; about 300 "delegates" from 47 states voting by state approved the Article V amendment 37-4 (4 abstaining), apportionment 26-10 (10) and Court of the Union 21-20 (5) after two hours of discussion. The proposals came from the National Legislative Conference's Committee on Federal-State Relations (chair Lloyd W. Lowrey) (Oberst 1964).

name: 1861 secession-crisis applications (KY, NJ, IL, IN, OH)
description: About five states applied Feb-Mar 1861 (NJ, KY, IL, IN, OH). Congress instead proposed the Corwin Amendment (Mar 2, 1861), which was not ratified.

name: American Bar Association House of Delegates vote on the CSG amendments (Aug 1963)
description: The ABA Board of Governors condemned the Article V and Court of the Union proposals on May 21, 1963. In August the House of Delegates amended committee resolutions so the ABA "disapproves and opposes" all three amendments, 136-74 on the apportionment motion, overriding a Committee on Jurisprudence and Law Reform (chair Louis Wyman) recommendation to approve the apportionment amendment (Oberst 1964). Several state and city bars also condemned them.
key_people: Louis Wyman (committee chair, recommended endorsing the apportionment amendment)

name: American Civil Liberties Union (national) opposition to the CSG amendments (1963)
description: The ACLU declared its opposition to the three CSG states-rights amendments on May 11, 1963 (Civil Liberties no. 208), per Oberst (1964). Distinct from the existing row for ACLU state affiliates.

name: Anti-polygamy convention application wave (1907-1915)
description: About 13 states applied for a convention to propose an anti-polygamy amendment (DE, SD, TN, WA, MT, NE, OH, VT, IL, OR, WI, MI, SC). No organizing group identified in sources opened. The list marks DE, TN, MT, OR and SC as later rescinded; WA rescinded all its prior applications in 2025 (SJM 8008).

name: Anti-Prohibition convention applications (1925-1932)
description: NV (1925) and MA, NY, WI, NJ (1931-32) applied for a convention to repeal Prohibition. Congress instead proposed the 21st Amendment (Blaine Act, Feb 20, 1933) for ratification by state conventions, the only amendment so ratified.

name: Direct election of senators application drive (1893-1911)
description: First application Nebraska 1893; spurts 1901-05 and 1907-11. Wikipedia: by 1912, 27 states had called for a convention. Senate passed the 17th Amendment June 12, 1911; ratified Apr 8, 1913. The 1907-11 spurt followed an interstate conference at Des Moines (Dec 5-6, 1906), called under an Iowa General Assembly resolution, which formed the Interstate Senatorial Convention to seek convention demands from the 37 legislatures meeting that winter (contemporary newspapers; UW catalog record).
key_people: Interstate Senatorial Convention (Des Moines, Dec 1906): Congressman Strode of Nebraska (president); Thomas A. Cheshire (executive committee chairman)

name: House Judiciary Committee hearing 'The Need for the Balanced Budget Amendment' (July 27 2017)
parent_or_affiliation: U.S. House Committee on the Judiciary
description: Full-committee hearing. The Compact for a Balanced Budget's administrator described the five-state compact route; Rep. Andy Biggs questioned whether the compact needs congressional consent.
key_people: Chair Bob Goodlatte; member witnesses Reps. John Ratcliffe, Bobby Scott, Vern Buchanan, Steve Stivers, Justin Amash, Barry Loudermilk, Stephanie Murphy; expert witnesses Douglas Holtz-Eakin (American Action Forum), Alan Blinder (Princeton), David Primo (Rochester), Nick Dranias (Compact for America)

name: House Judiciary Subcommittee on Civil and Constitutional Rights hearings on constitutional convention procedures (July 31 and Sept 23 1985)
parent_or_affiliation: U.S. House Committee on the Judiciary
description: 99th Congress hearings on Article V convention procedures. No House procedures bill reached the floor (CRS).

name: House Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution and Limited Government hearing 'Balancing the Federal Budget: Examining Proposals for a Balanced Budget Amendment' (Dec 3 2025)
parent_or_affiliation: U.S. House Committee on the Judiciary
description: BBA hearing whose witnesses included the leader of the push to compel a convention (FFSF). Chairman Jordan entered Rep. Arrington's Dec 12 2025 letter urging H.Con.Res. 15 into the record.
key_people: Subcommittee Chair Chip Roy; Chairman Jim Jordan; witnesses David M. Walker (FFSF), Kurt Couchman (Americans for Prosperity), Brittany Madni (Economic Policy Innovation Center), Brendan Duke (CBPP)

name: House Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution and Limited Government hearing 'Examining Proposed Constitutional Amendments' (Sept 19 2023)
parent_or_affiliation: U.S. House Committee on the Judiciary
description: Hearing that debated the convention route. Common Cause's Stephen Spaulding warned of an unlimited convention and dark money; Heritage's Thomas Jipping described subject-specific applications and the 38-state ratification check; Ranking Member Mary Gay Scanlon called the convention movement an astroturf effort.
key_people: Chair Mike Johnson (LA); Ranking Member Mary Gay Scanlon; witnesses Nick Tomboulides (U.S. Term Limits), David Primo, Stephen Spaulding (Common Cause), Thomas Jipping (Heritage)

name: Presidential term limits convention applications (1943)
description: Iowa, Illinois, Michigan and Wisconsin applied in 1943, after FDR's third term, for a convention on presidential tenure; Congress proposed the 22nd Amendment in 1947.

name: Proportional Electoral College convention applications (1963-1965)
description: About nine states (MT, AR, UT, CO, SD, WI, OK, NE, TX) applied for a convention on proportional allocation of electoral votes.

name: Revenue sharing convention applications (1949-1967)
description: Eleven states (12 applications, 1949-1967) applied for a convention on federal revenue sharing with the states; Congress later enacted revenue sharing by statute (1972). Link not established.

name: Right to Life convention application drive (1973-1980s)
description: State applications for a convention to propose a human life amendment reached 19 of the 34 needed by 1981 (Sager). Indiana was first: SJR 8 was adopted in the first regular session of the 98th General Assembly (1973) and printed in the Congressional Record on Feb 1, 1974 (Rep. Landgrebe's extension of remarks dated Jan 31, 1974), which explains the 1974 date in some sources. The Indiana text proposed state power to regulate abortion, and it would lapse if Congress proposed an identical amendment before June 1, 1975.

name: School busing / compulsory school assignment applications (1975-1984)
description: CRS (1985): during the 94th-98th Congresses, busing prompted 13 states to apply for a convention. Earlier 'School Management, States' Right' applications by GA, LA, MS and SC (1955-65) are listed separately.

name: School prayer convention applications (1975-1984)
description: CRS (1985): a movement to allow prayer in public schools produced five convention applications during the 94th-98th Congresses.

name: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Separation of Powers hearings on S. 2307 (Oct 30-31 1967)
parent_or_affiliation: U.S. Senate Committee on the Judiciary
description: Hearings on Ervin's bill to provide procedures for calling Article V conventions, held during the reapportionment application drive. Published by GPO in 1968. Witness list not verified.

name: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution hearing on S. 3, S. 520 and S. 1710 (Nov 29 1979)
parent_or_affiliation: U.S. Senate Committee on the Judiciary
description: Hearing on bills to provide procedures for calling Article V conventions, held as BBA applications approached 30 states. Published GPO 1980. Witness list not verified.

name: South Carolina and Georgia nullification-era applications (1832)
description: Georgia (Dec 1832) and South Carolina (Dec 1832) applied for a convention to clarify the Tenth Amendment, and Alabama (Jan 1833) sought a tariff limit. The crisis ended with the Compromise Tariff and Force Bill. GA and SC rescinded in 2004.

name: United States Conference of Mayors (1963 vote against the CSG amendments)
description: Voted on June 12, 1963 to denounce the three CSG states-rights amendments (Oberst 1964).

name: Washington Peace Conference (1861)
description: Called by Virginia in Jan 1861; 21 of 26 Union states sent delegates (Feb 4-27, 1861); proposed a 7-section amendment to Congress. Natelson treats it as a 'dry run' for an Article V convention, though it was not an Article V body.

name: Democracy Restated
description: Named as supporter of the National Constitution Center's 2025 Article V Project.
funding_notes: Funds NCC Article V Project

name: Koch-linked funder network (CMD aggregate)
description: Aggregate of Koch-connected grantmakers (DonorsTrust, Donors Capital Fund, Knowledge and Progress Fund, and others) as tallied by the Center for Media and Democracy.
funding_notes: CMD: Koch-linked groups gave nearly $5.4 million to Citizens for Self-Governance 2011-2015 (AlterNet Mar 24 2017). HuffPost (Apr 27 2021, citing CMD and Splinter IRS filings): parent org of COS received more than $12 million from Koch-linked groups and other major conservative donors 2010-2018. CMD estimate cited by The Guardian (Oct 19 2022): convention movement took in about $25 million in 2020.

name: Leonard Leo-linked groups (unnamed)
description: Business Insider (Aug 1 2022), citing CMD tax-filing research, says COS Action and CSG received money from groups connected to Leonard Leo; specific entities and amounts are not given in the excerpt.
funding_notes: Amount and year not disclosed in source. A separate Business Insider article (July 31 2022) reports that a 2020 internal audit of Convention of States showed a $1.3M Bitcoin donation made up 16% of its 2019 budget, and two donations totaling $2.5M made up 36% of its 2020 budget.

name: National Christian Charitable Foundation
description: Christian donor-advised fund sponsor (NCF). Its Form 990 Schedule I lists grants to Citizens for Self-Governance (Convention of States Foundation) in 9 of the 12 years 2013-2024. The stated purposes are generic categories, not Article V. The donors who advised the grants are not disclosed. Stance is unknown because a DAF sponsor acts on donor advice.
funding_notes: To Citizens for Self-Governance (EIN 27-1657203), Schedule I, purpose in brackets: TY2013 $125,000 [SOCIAL, CIVIC AND PUBLIC POLICY]; TY2015 $300; TY2016 $10,000; TY2017 $5,000 [JUSTICE]; TY2020 $357,400 [JUSTICE]; TY2021 $231,500 [JUSTICE]; TY2022 $287,035 [JUSTICE]; TY2023 $191,350 [JUSTICE]; TY2024 $130,600 [CIVIL RIGHTS]. Total $1,338,185. No CSG line in TY2014, TY2018 or TY2019. None of these grants is tied to Article V in the filing.

name: New World Foundation
parent_or_affiliation: 501(c)(3) public charity (files Form 990, not 990-PF), EIN 13-1919791, New York NY
description: Grantmaking public charity (files Form 990, not 990-PF). Its Form 990 for the year ending Sept 30 2024 lists a $50,000 grant to Common Cause with the stated purpose of supporting its work on Article V. Common Cause opposes an Article V convention, so the grant funds opposition work. Stance coded from that grant purpose only; no other Article V statement by the foundation was found.
funding_notes: FYE 2024-09-30 (Form 990 Schedule I): $50,000 to Common Cause (EIN 52-6078441), purpose "IN SUPPORT OF THEIR WORK ON ARTICLE V". Earlier grants to Common Cause (FYE 2018-2021: $75,000; $50,000; $50,000; $100,000; FYE 2023: $50,000) and to Common Cause Education Fund ($25,000, FYE 2018) carry the purpose "GENERAL SUPPORT" and are not tied to Article V. InfluenceWatch (secondary) reports the Article V grant as 2024.

name: Thomas W. Smith Foundation
description: Private foundation. Its 2017 Form 990-PF lists one $100,000 grant to Citizens for Self-Governance with the purpose "PUBLIC POLICY". No other grant to an Article V organization was found in its 2016-2017 or 2020-2024 filings. Stance is unknown because the grant is not tied to Article V in the filing.
funding_notes: TY2017 (990-PF): $100,000 to Citizens for Self-Governance, purpose "PUBLIC POLICY". Not tied to Article V in the filing.

name: FFSF draft complaint to compel an Article V convention call
role_title: Proposed state-plaintiff suit (not filed as of the March-April 2025 sources)
description: Draft suit, signed by Charles J. Cooper, claiming Congress was obliged to call a convention because the two-thirds threshold was met in 1979, and that rescissions cannot undo applications ('once the Article V bell has been rung, it cannot be unrung'). FFSF met the Utah AG's office (2023) and planned a meeting with Texas AG Ken Paxton; Alaska is listed on the draft complaint but its AG would not confirm; West Virginia introduced a resolution to commence federal court action; Arizona and South Carolina lawmakers sought participation. As of the March 2025 ProPublica report, Walker said he hoped states would announce their intent to sue within two months and file shortly after.
key_people: David M. Walker (FFSF chair); David Biddulph (his organization became FFSF); Charles 'Chuck' Cooper (counsel)

name: Sibley v. McConnell, 139 F. Supp. 3d 194 (D.D.C. 2015)
parent_or_affiliation: U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia
role_title: Federal suit (removed from D.C. Superior Court)
description: Pro se plaintiff Montgomery Blair Sibley sought mandamus compelling Majority Leader McConnell and Speaker Boehner to call a convention, claiming 35 states had applied. Judge Boasberg remanded to D.C. Superior Court for lack of Article III standing (generalized grievance) on Oct 13 2015.
key_people: Montgomery Blair Sibley (plaintiff); Sen. Mitch McConnell, Rep. John Boehner (defendants); Judge James E. Boasberg

role_title: Registered lobbyist for Convention of States Action

role_title: Registered lobbyist for U.S. Term Limits

role_title: Registered lobbyist for U.S. Term Limits

role_title: Registered lobbyist for Convention of States Action

role_title: Registered lobbyist for U.S. Term Limits

role_title: Registered lobbyist for U.S. Term Limits

name: Sean Grehalva
role_title: Registered lobbyist for U.S. Term Limits

name: Carter administration (Vice President Walter Mondale's office)
description: Morgan (1998) says the Carter administration and congressional Democrats stalled the drive at 30 states. CRS (R42592) reports that the counter-convention group Citizens for the Constitution described the NTU effort as a stealth campaign, and quotes Mondale's chief of staff: 'They were remarkably successful until it became known what they were doing.'

name: Committee on Federal-State Relations, National Legislative Conference (1962)
parent_or_affiliation: National Legislative Conference (Council of State Governments affiliate)
role_title: Drafting committee for the three 1962-63 states-rights amendments
description: Nine-member committee appointed by NLC chairman W. Stuart Helm after the Phoenix meeting (Sept. 1962); drafted the three amendments (amending Article V, Court of the Union, apportionment) and the plan for every legislature to pass three uniform convention applications on Jan. 16, 1963. Its report went to the 16th Biennial General Assembly of the States, Chicago, Dec. 6-7, 1962, which approved the proposals 37-4, 26-10 and 21-20 (Oberst 1964). Oberst notes the Speakers of TX, MO, IL and FL and Assemblyman Hauser of NJ had sat on the committee, and those states acted early.
key_people: Lloyd W. Lowrey (CA, chairman); William Chappell Jr. (FL Speaker); Warren Wood (former IL Speaker); James Turman (TX Speaker); Thomas D. Graham (MO Speaker); Robert D. Haase (WI Speaker); Clarence L. Carpenter (AZ Senate President); Frank King (OH); Frederick H. Hauser (NJ)

name: Compact for a Balanced Budget Commission
parent_or_affiliation: Compact for a Balanced Budget (interstate compact)
description: Commission established Jan 2015 under the interstate Compact for a Balanced Budget (five member states per CRS 2017; named in Dranias's July 27 2017 House Judiciary testimony as AK, AZ, GA, MS, ND). Its compact administrator, Nick Dranias, testified to House Judiciary July 27 2017. Congressional consent sought via H.Con.Res. 26 (114th) and H.Con.Res. 73 (115th); not given. || Commission of member states established Jan 2015 under the Compact for a Balanced Budget.
funding_notes: Received $88,500 (2015) and $57,979 (2016) from the Compact for America Educational Foundation (its Schedule I), to fund commission activities, mainly travel to educate state legislators and members of Congress.

name: Congressional Research Service - Article V convention reports
description: Main official analyses of the convention route: IB80062 (1985); R42592 (2012) and R42589 (Thomas Neale, 2016); R44435 (Neale, Nov 15 2017; tracked claimed counts by campaign and the House Clerk list); R48466 (Hudiburg, Mar 20 2025; House rule change).
key_people: Thomas H. Neale; Jane A. Hudiburg (R48466 author)

name: Joint Committee on the Economic Report and House Select Committee on Small Business (1952 staff study)
description: Feb 1952 joint committee print 'Constitutional Limitation on Federal Income, Estate, and Gift Tax Rates' (82d Cong.) analyzed the 14-year drive: began 1938; first application Wyoming 1939; 25-plus claimed, 'probably no more than 15' in force after rescissions and form defects.
key_people: Arthur F. Lucas (Small Business Committee staff)

name: National Archives and Records Administration - Center for Legislative Archives
description: Holds Article V applications in scattered collections; there is no central repository (CRS). Wikipedia reports a Mar 12 2007 National Archives letter to Sen. Bernie Sanders on the subject (contents not verified). H.R. 1742 (115th) and H.R. 8419 (117th) would have made NARA or the Archivist compile and count applications; neither was enacted. The Archivist's statutory Article V role is certifying ratified amendments (1 U.S.C. 106b).

name: National Federalism Commission (NFC; formerly Phoenix Correspondence Commission)
parent_or_affiliation: Created by the 2017 Phoenix BBA Planning Convention
description: Created as the Phoenix Correspondence Commission (PCC) by the 2017 Phoenix convention to liaise with Congress, track applications, propose a time and place for a convention, and arrange legal representation; renamed NFC in 2025. Up to 100 delegates (one per legislative chamber; two from Nebraska). Federal Fiscal Sustainability Foundation chair David Walker testified that NFC began working with House Judiciary in early 2025 to update application records. The NFC separately says it reached an agreement with the Committee; no signed agreement was located in this audit. Its Sept. 17, 2025 analysis claims 34+ fiscal-plus-plenary applications were active 1979-2004 and again 2016-2017. Status as a government body rests on its own description. || The NFC Who's Who roster (fetched 2026-10-03) lists 60 named state delegates from 37 states, plus one Utah seat marked 'TBD'. It says 'Additional delegates are in process.' Its 'Be an NFC Delegate' page says a delegate need not be a sitting legislator. Its funding page says it is 'funded by the States' and points donors to Citizens Voice, a 501(c)(3). Full roster in expand2_official_notes.md.
key_people: W. Bruce Lee (executive director) || Officers per NFC Who's Who (fetched 2026-10-03): Mark Lepak (President); Shelley Hughes (Vice President); David Guldenschuh (Secretary); Rex Rice (Treasurer); W. Bruce Lee (Executive Director). Board of Scholars: Andrew Bibby; David Guldenschuh; Donald J. Kochan; Lawrence Lessig; Robert G. Natelson; Jodey Arrington.

name: Office of the Clerk, U.S. House of Representatives - Selected Memorials (Article V)
description: Posts Judiciary-designated Article V applications and rescissions, 1960 onward, by year and state. CRS (Nov 2017) counted 134 applications from 46 states and 21 rescissions from 20 states. As of fetch 2026-10-03 the newest entries were OK 2023 and TN 2024; 2025-26 rescissions (CA, CT, WA, MA) and KS and AZ applications do not appear. H.Con.Res. 15 would assign the Clerk a 60-day certification role.

name: U.S. House Rule XII clause 3(b) (Article V memorials designation; orig. H.Res. 5 114th Cong. sec. 3(c))
description: Separate order adopted Jan 6 2015 and codified as a standing rule in the 119th Congress (Jan 3 2025): the Judiciary chair shall designate Article V application and rescission memorials from the 114th Congress on (and may designate earlier ones); the Clerk posts them by state and year, marked as application or rescission. Designation is for public availability; the Clerk's list describes each memorial as one that 'purports to be an application.'

name: U.S. Senate - petitions and memorials (POM) practice for Article V applications
description: Applications are laid before the Senate as petitions or memorials, given POM numbers, printed in the Congressional Record and referred to Judiciary.

name: AFL-CIO
description: Signer of 2017 national letter; opposes the balanced budget amendment on fiscal grounds (2018 letter on H.J.Res. 2 citing CBPP). State federations (AK, CO, ID, IA, KS, KY, ME, MA, MN, MS, MT, NH, ND, OK, SC, SD, VA, WA, WI, WY, MD-DC) signed the 2017 and 2017-MD letters.

name: Alliance for Justice
description: Coalition signer opposing Article V convention calls and urging rescission. Signer of 2017 national letter.

name: American Bar Association Special Constitutional Convention Study Committee (1974 report)
description: Report 'Amendment of the Constitution by the Convention Method Under Article V' (1974): Congress's duty to call is mandatory; limited conventions are permissible; rescission allowed before the threshold; delegates apportioned one person, one vote; governors have no role; endorsed S. 1272 with amendments. || Produced Amendment of the Constitution by the Convention Method Under Article V (1974): concluded a convention could be limited, Congress could legislate procedures, the duty to call is mandatory once the threshold is validly met, and delegates must be apportioned one person, one vote.

name: American Civil Liberties Union (state affiliates)
description: ACLU affiliates testify against convention applications on the ground that a convention could be co-opted and endanger the Bill of Rights; documented in MA (2018, 2025), MD (2018), WV (2018), MO (2021), ME (2024).
key_people: Carol Rose; Gavi Wolfe; Joanna Diamond; Eli Baumwell; Meagan Sway

name: American Constitution Society
description: Publishes opposition scholarship (Super's A Dangerous Adventure, 2021) and hosts programs such as Weaponizing Article V: An Emerging Threat to our Constitution; its president Russ Feingold co-wrote The Constitution in Jeopardy (2022). || Runs an Article V project opposing convention efforts as a 'radical effort' by 'factions of the far Right'; published Super's 2021 policy brief and Feingold & Prindiville's 2022 book; held speaking tours in NH, MA, CA, IL, PA and other states.

name: American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME)
description: Signer of 2017 national letter; councils and locals in AZ, IA, MD, MA, NV, WI signed state letters. 2014 convention resolution opposes a balanced budget amendment.

name: American Legislative Exchange Council (ALEC) - Task Force on Federalism and International Relations
description: ALEC task force on federalism; ALEC maintains Article V model policies: Application for a Convention of the States; Compact for America Balanced Budget Amendment; Resolution for a Federal Balanced Budget Amendment; a model on rules of procedure for an Article V convention (Jan 2016); publishes an Article V handbook for state lawmakers. ALEC reaffirmed support for Article V initiatives in a Feb 11 2016 letter-related post addressed to House Judiciary Chairman Goodlatte.
key_people: Karla Jones (task force director); Sen. Leah Vukmir (WI; 2016 national chair); Speaker Linda Upmeyer (IA; chair, Center to Restore the Balance of Government); Lisa B. Nelson (CEO)
funding_notes: ProPublica/PBS Wisconsin report FFSF has drawn support from ALEC; VOA (2017) names ALEC and Americans for Prosperity as backers of Phoenix convention push

name: American Promise
parent_or_affiliation: Listed partner of State Legislators Article V Caucus
description: Cross-partisan campaign for the For Our Freedom Amendment (campaign-spending limits), pursued through Congress and state ratification rather than a convention. Claims 25 states are 'ready-to-ratify'. || Founded 2016 by Jeff Clements to win the For Our Freedom Amendment; uses state resolutions urging Congress to propose it (25 states listed by Wikipedia) plus federal lobbying, not an Article V convention.

name: American Taxpayers Association
description: Listed by the 1952 joint committee print among advocates of the 25% limit: its Tax Information Series covered the amendment; published 'Why the 25 Percent Limit on Federal Taxes' (1944) and reprinted D. E. Casey's 'Federal Taxing Power must be Limited.'

name: Americans For Fair Taxation
description: Created the FairTax plan (first introduced in Congress July 14, 1999), which would need repeal of the 16th Amendment. No Article V convention activity found.

name: ArticleV.org

Planning subcommittee asked Congress to convene within 180 days of the 34th application; created the Phoenix Correspondence Commission; called for another gathering before Dec 31 2018. parent_or_affiliation: U.S. District Court for the District of Kansas
description: Section 1983 suit filed Dec 22, 2023 by Sen. Judge Toby Crouse held Article V permits no state-imposed limit (terminated Nov 5, 2025), clearing SCR 1604, which the House adopted 80-42 on Jan 22, 2026. || Kansas Sen. Mike Thompson and Michael Murphy (a House member when suit was filed, per the opinion; called a senator in Nov 2025 coverage) sued Senate President Ty Masterson and House Speaker Dan Hawkins, who had declared Convention of States resolutions lost for missing the state-constitutional two-thirds vote. name: Sam J. Ervin Jr.
description: Responding to the Dirksen campaign, introduced the Federal Constitutional Convention Procedures Act in the 90th Congress to set rules for any convention. Successors passed the Senate: S. 215 (92nd) by 84-0 in 1971 and S. 1272 (93rd) on July 9, 1973. The House never acted. The 92nd and 93rd Congress bills kept applications in effect for seven years, allowed states to rescind them, limited a convention to its called subject, and let Congress reject disfavored convention proposals. description: HJ 7 (2019; Reps. Edwards, Jennings; Sens. Anderson, Hutchings) would have rescinded a prior Wyoming resolution requesting an Article V convention; House Judiciary recommended do pass 5-4 but it was not considered in committee of the whole. HJ 5 (2020; Reps. Edwards, Jennings, Styvar, Tass, Wilson, Winter; Sen. Hutchings) failed introduction 13-47.

name: Wyoming single-subject and countermand applications (2017-2018)
description: H.J. 3 (2017, Laursen; single-subject amendment) passed the House 33-24 and died uncalled in the Senate; S.J. 5 (2017, Peterson; countermand amendment) failed Senate third reading 13-17; H.J. 3 (2018, single subject) failed introduction 26-33; H.J. 10 (2018, Laursen; convention for proposing amendments) was not considered for introduction.

name: Wyoming SJ 5 (2026) Convention of States resolution
description: 'Convention of states.' Lead sponsor Sen. Driskill with Sens. Case, Crum, Kolb, Laursen and Olsen and Reps. Banks, Clouston and Williams. Introduced 21-10 (Feb 11, 2026); Senate Judiciary do pass 5-0; Senate third reading 19-12 (Feb 24); House Education do pass 5-3-1; failed House committee of the whole 21-28-7-6 (Mar 3, 2026). Successor to SJ 1 (2025), already covered in the 2019-2025 event row.

role_title: Registered lobbyist for U.S. Term Limits

description: The Governor signed both Wyoming's 2009 repeal of all prior Article V applications (HEJR No. 3, March 11, 2009) and its 2017 balanced budget amendment application (HEJR No. 2, March 17, 2017).

name: Wyoming Article V delegate limits statute (HB 50, Enrolled Act 123, 2017)
role_title: Statutory delegate limits and oath penalties
description: HB 0050 (2017) creates W.S. 9-22-101 and 9-22-102, "Limitations on Delegates to a Convention for Proposing Amendments," with penalties for violating the delegate oath (a felony per the enrolled text). Enrolled Act 123; LSO record shows "Governor Signed HEA No. 0123" and chapter CH0197 on March 14, 2017 (signedDate field reads 3/13/2017); effective July 1, 2017.
key_people: Rep. Laursen (sponsor); Reps. Allen, Lindholm, Winters

name: Wyoming House Committee on Education
description: Committee of House referral for Wyoming's Convention of States resolutions; recommended do pass on SJ 1 (2025) 6-3 (ayes Andrew, Erickson, Kelly, Lawley, Singh, Williams; nays Bratten, Guggenmos, Strock) and SJ 5 (2026) 5-3. Both then failed in House committee of the whole.

name: Austin "Kit" Jennings
description: Senate co-sponsor of Wyoming H.J. 7 (2009, HEJR 3), repealing all prior Article V applications; voted aye on Senate passage (25-5).

name: Bruce Burns
description: Senate sponsor of Wyoming H.J. 7 (2009, HEJR 3), the repeal of all prior Article V applications; author of the adopted Senate amendment declaring the applications 'repealed, rescinded, canceled, nullified and voided'.

name: Cale Case
description: Senate co-sponsor of Wyoming's 2017 balanced budget application (H.J. 2, enacted), the single-subject applications H.J. 3 (2017, 2018), the countermand application S.J. 5 (2017) and Convention of States resolutions SJ 4 (2019), SJ 2 (2021), HJ 2 (2022), SJ 11 (2023), HJ 6 / SJ 4 (2024) and SJ 5 (2026).

name: Clifford Jennings
description: Co-sponsor of Wyoming rescission resolutions HJ 7 (2019) and HJ 5 (2020).

name: Daniel Laursen
description: As a representative: co-sponsor H.J. 4 (2015) and H.J. 2 (2017, balanced budget, enacted); lead sponsor H.J. 3 (2017, single-subject amendment; passed House 33-24, not considered in Senate COW), H.J. 3 (2018, failed introduction 26-33), H.J. 10 (2018, not considered), HJ 12 (2021, Convention of States, not considered) and HJ 2 (2022, failed introduction 21-37). As a senator: lead sponsor SJ 11 (2023, passed Senate 17-13, failed House COW 21-41) and SJ 5 (2025, congressional term limits, died in committee); co-sponsor SJ 4 (2024), SJ 1 (2025), SJ 5 (2026). || Sponsor of HB 0050 (2017), limitations on Article V delegates (W.S. 9-22-101, -102), Enrolled Act 123, signed by the governor March 2017. || Listed as a Wyoming state delegate on the National Federalism Commission roster (nfcommission.gov/whos-who, fetched 2026-10-03).

name: Daniel Singh
description: Listed as a WY state delegate on the National Federalism Commission (NFC) 'Who's Who' roster (fetched 2026-10-03). The NFC says each legislative chamber appoints its own delegate and that delegates need not be sitting legislators. No NFC bio page; office not stated on the roster. Roster listing alone is not evidence of stance.

name: Dennis Biteman
description: Co-sponsor of Wyoming S.J. 5 (2017, countermand) as a representative; as a senator, lead sponsor of SJ 2 (2021, Convention of States, failed COW 14-16) and co-sponsor of SJ 4 (2019), HJ 2 (2022), SJ 11 (2023), HJ 6 and SJ 4 (2024) and SJ 1 (2025); voted aye on SJ 1 (2025) and SJ 5 (2026).

name: Eric Barlow
role_title: State Senator; primary sponsor of SJ0001 (2025)
description: Primary sponsor of Wyoming SJ0001 (2025), a Convention of States application (term limits, federal spending, federal regulation), after several earlier failed Wyoming attempts; voted aye on the 2026 successor SJ0005, which failed in the House.

name: Evie Brennan
description: Lead sponsor of Wyoming SJ 4 (2024), 'Convention of states-2', which failed introduction 17-14; co-sponsor of SJ 11 (2023) and SJ 1 (2025).

name: Gary Crum
description: Co-sponsor of Wyoming SJ 5 (2026), Convention of States; Senate Judiciary member who voted do pass on SJ 1 (2025) and SJ 5 (2026) and aye on Senate passage of both.

name: Hutchings (WY Senate)
description: Senate sponsor of Wyoming rescission resolutions HJ 7 (2019) and HJ 5 (2020); voted nay on Senate passage of the Convention of States resolutions SJ 1 (2025) and SJ 5 (2026).

name: James Anderson
description: Senate co-sponsor of Wyoming HJ 7 (2019), rescinding a prior Article V request; voted nay on Senate passage of Convention of States resolutions SJ 1 (2025) and SJ 5 (2026). Full name per the Wyoming Legislature's legislator roster.

name: Jared Olsen
description: Lead sponsor of Wyoming HJ 6 (2024), Convention of States (not considered for introduction); co-sponsor of SJ 4 (2019), SJ 2 (2021), HJ 2 (2022), SJ 11 (2023), SJ 4 (2024), SJ 1 (2025) and SJ 5 (2026). As a senator he sat on Senate Judiciary, which recommended SJ 1 (2025) and SJ 5 (2026) do pass 5-0.

name: JD Williams
description: House co-sponsor of Wyoming SJ 1 (2025) and SJ 5 (2026), Convention of States; voted do pass in House Education and aye in committee of the whole on both (failed 25-32 and 21-28).

name: Jeff Wasserburger
description: Lead sponsor of Wyoming SJ 4 (2019), 'Proposing amendments through a convention of states' (failed committee of the whole 10-20), and SJ 2 (2019), a free and fair elections convention application that failed in Senate Minerals 2-3; co-sponsor of H.J. 4 (2015) and H.J. 2 (2017, balanced budget, enacted), H.J. 10 (2018), SJ 2 (2021) and HJ 2 (2022).

name: John Kolb
description: Co-sponsor of Wyoming Convention of States resolutions SJ 11 (2023), HJ 6 and SJ 4 (2024), SJ 1 (2025) and SJ 5 (2026), and of the 2025 term-limits application SJ 5; as a Senate Judiciary member voted do pass on SJ 1 (2025) and SJ 5 (2026).

name: Ken Clouston
description: House co-sponsor of Wyoming Convention of States resolutions SJ 11 (2023), SJ 1 (2025) and SJ 5 (2026); voted aye on SJ 1 in committee of the whole (failed 25-32, Feb 28, 2025); excused on the SJ 5 vote (failed 21-28, March 3, 2026).

name: Nathan Winters
description: Lead sponsor of Wyoming H.J. 1 (2017), 'Convention for proposing constitutional amendments', which failed in House committee of the whole 18-42 on Jan 30, 2017; co-sponsor of H.J. 2 (2017, balanced budget, enacted), SJ 5 (2017, countermand) and H.J. 10 (2018).

name: Ogden Driskill
role_title: State Senator; lead sponsor of SJ 5 (2026)
description: Lead sponsor (with Sens. Case, Crum, Kolb, Laursen, Olsen and Reps. Banks, Clouston, Williams) of Wyoming SJ0005 (2026), 'Convention of states'; passed Senate 19-12 Feb 24, 2026; House Education Committee recommended do pass 5-3; failed in House committee of the whole 21-28 on Mar 3, 2026. Also co-sponsor of SJ 1 (2025, Convention of States; passed Senate 22-7, failed House committee of the whole 25-32) and SJ 5 (2025, congressional term limits; failed Senate Judiciary 2-3).

name: Ray Peterson
description: Lead sponsor of Wyoming S.J. 5 (2017), an Article V application for a 'countermand amendment', which failed Senate third reading 13-17 on Jan 24, 2017; Senate co-sponsor of H.J. 1 and H.J. 2 (2017) and H.J. 10 (2018).

name: Robert Brechtel
role_title: State Representative; lead sponsor of H.J. 7 (2009)
description: Lead sponsor of Wyoming H.J. 7 (2009), enacted as HEJR No. 3, repealing all of Wyoming's prior requests for an Article V convention.

name: Roy Edwards
description: Lead sponsor of Wyoming HJ 7 (2019) and HJ 5 (2020), joint resolutions rescinding a previous Wyoming request to Congress for an Article V convention; HJ 7 cleared House Judiciary 5-4 but was not considered on the floor; HJ 5 failed introduction 13-47.

name: Tyler Lindholm
description: Lead sponsor of Wyoming's balanced budget amendment applications H.J. 4 (2015, failed in Senate 7-22) and H.J. 2 (2017, enacted as HEJR No. 2); co-sponsor of the single-subject applications H.J. 3 (2017, 2018), of H.J. 10 (2018), a convention application for amendments "as specified", and of the 2019 Convention of States resolution SJ 4.
